days.paraphrase: If it isn't right, don't do it; if it isn't true, don't say it. Let your effort be...

apply.work: What at work isn't quite right that you're doing anyway?
apply.family: What isn't quite true that you've been saying at home?
apply.decision: Test each option: is it right? Is what you'll say about it true?

days.context: Marcus names the four cardinal virtues, justice, truth, temperance and courage, and challenges himself to find anything better.
days.paraphrase: If you find anything in life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, and a mind content with acting by right reason, turn to it with your whole soul. But if nothing looks better than the god within you, don't give room to anything else, such as praise, power, wealth or pleasure. Choose the better, freely and simply, and hold to it.

apply.work: What at work are you tempted to rank above justice or truth?
apply.family: What at home competes with the four virtues for your attention?
apply.decision: Which option would you choose if nothing ranked above the four virtues?

days.context: A companion to 6.21. Marcus insists that changing your mind is itself an act of freedom.

keyword.gloss: to change one's mind, to shift position

days.paraphrase: Remember that changing your mind and following someone who corrects you is as free as persisting in error. It's still your own act, done by your own judgement and understanding.

apply.work: Where at work are you holding a position because changing it feels like losing?
apply.family: What would changing your mind at home, freely, look like?
apply.decision: Would changing your mind about this decision be a loss, or a free choice?

days.context: Marcus's advice on falling short: philosophy isn't a stern schoolmaster but a soothing remedy, like a bathe for sore eyes.
days.paraphrase: Don't be disgusted, discouraged or dissatisfied if you don't always act on right principles. When you fail, come back, and be content if most of what you do fits human nature. Love what you return to. Don't go back to philosophy as to a harsh master, but as someone with sore eyes goes to a soothing remedy.

apply.work: Where have you fallen short at work lately? What would returning, without disgust, look like?
apply.family: At home, how do you treat yourself after a bad day?
apply.decision: If this decision goes wrong, how will you return, rather than give up?

days.context: Marcus tells himself to stop studying other people's minds and look straight at his own path, set by nature.

keyword.gloss: nature, the way a thing is made to grow

days.paraphrase: Don't look around at other people's ruling minds. Look straight at where nature leads you: nature as a whole, through what happens to you, and your own, through what you must do. Everything should act by its make, and ours is made first for community, then for resisting the body's pulls, then for not being misled.

apply.work: Whose path at work are you watching instead of your own?
apply.family: At home, whose choices are you comparing yourself to?
apply.decision: Looking only at where your nature leads, what's your choice?

days.context: The opening of the final book. Everything you're trying to reach by a roundabout route is available now, if you stop refusing it.

keyword.gloss: a going round, a roundabout way

days.paraphrase: All that you're trying to reach by a roundabout road you can have now, if you don't refuse it to yourself: let go of the past, trust the future to providence, and direct the present by reverence and justice. Fear not that your life will end, but that it will never have begun according to nature.

apply.work: What at work are you reaching by a roundabout road that you could simply do now?
apply.family: What would beginning to live by nature, at home, look like this week?
apply.decision: What does this decision look like if you take the direct road?

days.context: Book 11 opens by listing what the rational soul does: it sees, analyses and shapes itself. Its work is complete at every moment, not only at the end.
days.paraphrase: The rational soul sees itself, examines itself, and makes itself what it chooses. It enjoys its own fruit. It reaches its end wherever life stops, unlike a dance or a play that's incomplete if cut short. At every point it can say: I have what is mine.

apply.work: Which part of your work is complete in itself, even if the project ends tomorrow?
apply.family: What at home is already whole, without waiting for some future milestone?
apply.decision: If this decision were your last act, would it be complete in itself?

days.context: The last passage of the Meditations. Marcus compares life to a play: three acts can be the whole drama, and the one who ends it is satisfied.

keyword.gloss: city, state, the community one belongs to

days.paraphrase: You've been a citizen of this great city, the world. What does it matter whether for five years or three? What's lawful is fair to all. Nature, which brought you in, sends you out, like a praetor dismissing an actor. But I've only played three of the five acts. True, but in life three acts are the whole play. Leave content, for the one who releases you is content.

apply.work: If your work stopped after act three, would it be a whole play?
apply.family: What would it mean to be content with your family life as a complete drama so far?
apply.decision: Make your last decision of this course as a citizen of the world. What do you choose?
